descriptor: An orange-and-black butterfly that flies thousands of kilometres to spend winter in Mexican fir forests.

range.summary: Breeds across southern Canada and the United States wherever milkweed grows. Eastern monarchs overwinter in central Mexico and western monarchs on the California coast.
regions: Midwest and Great Lakes breeding range
Oyamel fir forests of Michoacan and Mexico State

population.unit: hectares of forest occupied by overwintering eastern monarchs in Mexico (December survey)

source.label: WWF Mexico and CONANP overwintering survey

population.note: Each year is the winter season that starts that December, so 2025 means 2025 to 2026. Surveys before 2004 were made by the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve. Researchers suggest about 6 hectares is needed for a resilient eastern population.

threats.title: Migratory subspecies at risk
threats.detail: The species is Least Concern worldwide, but the migratory North American subspecies, D. p. plexippus, is listed separately as Vulnerable (2023).

threats.title: Milkweed loss
threats.detail: Herbicide use and land conversion have stripped milkweed, the only food of monarch caterpillars, from much of the breeding range.

threats.title: Forest degradation in Mexico
threats.detail: Logging and drought thin the oyamel fir canopy that shelters the winter colonies from cold.

threats.title: Climate extremes
threats.detail: Heat, drought and winter storms along the migration route kill butterflies and dry up nectar sources.

places.name: El Rosario Sanctuary
places.note: The largest colony of the 2025 to 2026 season, high in the oyamel forest of Michoacan.

places.name: Sierra Chincua Sanctuary
places.note: Quieter sanctuary in the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, reached on foot or horseback.

places.name: Point Pelee National Park
places.note: Monarchs gather at the tip of the point in September before crossing Lake Erie.

places.name: Cape May Point
places.note: Autumn migrants pile up here before crossing Delaware Bay.

places.name: Pismo Beach Monarch Butterfly Grove
places.note: Eucalyptus grove used by the separate western population.

sightings.tip: Mexican sanctuaries are at their best from December to February, on sunny afternoons when clusters break into flight. Autumn migration peaks along the Great Lakes and Atlantic coast in September.

actions.title: Plant native milkweed
actions.detail: Grow a milkweed species native to your region, plus late-blooming nectar flowers for migrants.

actions.title: Garden without pesticides
actions.detail: Insecticides and herbicides kill caterpillars directly and remove the plants they need.

actions.title: Tag and report monarchs
actions.detail: Community science tagging and sighting reports track the migration each year.

actions.title: Visit sanctuaries with local guides
actions.detail: Tourism income gives the ejidos that own the forests a reason to protect them.

regions.name: Michoacan fir forests
regions.note: Eastern monarchs cluster in oyamel fir forests here each winter, on just a few hectares.

regions.name: Monterey Bay groves
regions.note: Pacific Grove counted no monarchs in 2020, then about 12,000 returned in 2021.

regions.name: Central Coast groves
regions.note: Only 1,914 western monarchs were counted in California in 2020 before a rebound in 2021.

regions.name: Midwest breeding range
regions.note: The Midwest is a key summer breeding area for the eastern migratory population.

regions.name: Great Lakes and Ontario
regions.note: Summer breeding reaches north into southern Ontario and Quebec wherever milkweed grows.

regions.name: Texas
regions.note: Spring migrants from Mexico lay the first generation of eggs on milkweed across Texas.

regions.name: Western breeding range
regions.note: Western monarchs breed inland across the Great Basin and the Pacific Northwest.

regions.name: Eastern Australia
regions.note: Monarchs were first recorded in Australia in 1871, in Queensland and near Melbourne.

regions.name: Canary Islands
regions.note: Monarchs had established themselves in the Canary Islands by about 1880.

regions.name: Southern Spain
regions.note: The first Iberian breeding was recorded in southern Spain in the late 1960s.

regions.name: Azores
regions.note: Monarchs first bred in the Azores on Faial in 1994 and on more islands by 2000.

regions.name: Algarve, Portugal
regions.note: Breeding was first confirmed on mainland Portugal in the Algarve in 2003.

source.label: US Fish and Wildlife Service, Monarch Species Status Assessment Report v2.1

rangeHistory.note: No whole region has been lost; the steep declines show in the population chart rather than as lost areas.
